e: Borrowed from Latin ēvulsiōnem, from ēvellere.
q: Herein, therefore, to speak compendiously, we first presume to affirm that, from a strict enquiry, we cannot maintain the evulsion or biting off any parts [...].
1646, Sir Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica, III.4:
or be preſented to the view of my country, being (I confeſſe) so much the more doubtfull to euulge the ſame, by how much the more I am no scholar
after the intrinsical and most researched secrets of the grammar and lexicon which I am about to evulge.

e: From Latin evulgatus, past participle of evulgare (“to publish”).
